story880:
In the beginning, there was a world before this one — a world of monsters and darkness, where beings of terrible power stalked the land and devoured anything that dared to live. Then came the great flood, sent by forces older than the monsters themselves, and the old world was washed clean.

After the flood, White Painted Woman appeared. She was Change itself — her body shifting with the seasons, her hair flowing between white and brown and black as the months turned. She was identified with the Moon and with Thunder, for she controlled the cycles that governed all life.

The Sun looked down upon White Painted Woman and was moved. Rays of light touched her, and she conceived. From this union was born Child of the Water — a boy who emerged from the waves already powerful, already knowing his purpose.

Child of the Water became the dominant culture hero of the Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache. He was sometimes described as the Sun himself in another form, and his younger brother, the Wise One, walked beside him.

Together they journeyed through the world, ridding it of the monsters that survived the flood. Child of the Water fought with weapons of lightning and stone, and where he walked, the land healed. Rivers ran clean. Plants grew. The people, who had been hiding in caves and canyons, emerged and followed in his footsteps.

White Painted Woman watched from above, her power flowing through the land like water through roots. Her first menstruation — the moment when her power became fully manifest — was reenacted in the Girls' Puberty Ceremony, the most sacred ritual of Apache life.

The ceremony lasts four days. On the first day, the young woman is painted with white clay, just as White Painted Woman was painted by the Sun. On the second day, she dances with the Mountain Spirits — the Gahe — who bless her with health and fertility. On the third day, she runs eastward toward the rising Sun, carrying a basket of sacred objects. On the fourth day, she is released into womanhood, her transformation complete.

The ceremony ensures that the young woman carries White Painted Woman's power into the future, just as she carried it from the old world into the new.
story881:
In Lipan Apache tradition, the story of creation begins not with a single act but with a journey — a movement from chaos to order that mirrors the journey every human life must make.

Killer-of-Enemies was the primary creator and culture hero, identified with the Sun. He was the child of Changing Woman, who was herself identified as the Moon and Thunder. From his first breath, Killer-of-Enemies understood his purpose: to make the world safe for the people who would come after him.

He journeyed through the world alone, establishing the proper order of things. Where the rivers ran backwards, he turned them. Where the mountains leaned dangerously, he straightened them. Where monsters lurked in the shadows, he destroyed them with weapons forged from lightning.

He had a younger brother called Wise One, who was smaller but cleverer. Wise One could see things that Killer-of-Enemies missed — the subtle trap, the hidden weakness, the path that looked wrong but was right. Together they were unstoppable.

Killer-of-Enemies defeated powerful enemies — giant animals and spirits who threatened the people. He fought the great serpent who lived in the river and caused floods. He fought the stone monster who blocked the sun. He fought the darkness itself, pushing it back until the sky was clear.

His battles established the sacred geography of the Lipan Apache world. Each mountain he climbed became a sacred site. Each river he crossed became a place of ceremony. The landscape was not merely physical but spiritual — a map of the hero's journey from chaos to order.

After completing his work, Killer-of-Enemies departed. He climbed into the sky and became the Sun, rising each morning to remind the people that darkness is temporary and light always returns.

Before he left, he made a promise: "If you ever truly need me, I will return."

The Lipan Apache remember this promise in their ceremonies. When the Sun Dance is performed, when the sacred fire is lit, when the prayers rise with the smoke, Killer-of-Enemies hears. And though he does not come back in body, his power flows through the light that warms the earth, the fire that cooks the food, the spark that ignites the heart.
story882:
In the White Mountain Apache creation myth recorded by Noze in 1910, a maiden climbed to the top of a high mountain where the rays of the rising Sun first struck the earth. She raised her skirt and the breath of the Sun entered her. She went up the mountain four mornings, and four times the Sun's breath entered her.

This unmarried girl became pregnant, and the people gossiped about her. Their whispers were sharp as thorns, and the maiden bore their judgment in silence, for she knew what she carried was not shame but purpose.

She gave birth to twins: Naiyenezgani — Monster Slayer — and Tobatc'istcini — Child of the Water. The boys grew with supernatural speed, their bodies strengthening with each sunrise, their weapons growing heavier in their hands.

Their father the Sun sent them gifts — weapons of power, shields that could turn aside any blow, arrows that flew straighter than any human could shoot. The twins received these gifts and understood their destiny: they were born to rid the world of monsters.

Naiyenezgani was the elder, and he was bold. He walked into the territory of Naiye', a monster that devoured humans, and challenged it to single combat. The earth shook as they fought. Naiye' was enormous, its teeth like daggers, its claws like scythes. But Naiyenezgani's weapon found its mark, and the monster fell.

Tobatc'istcini was quieter but no less powerful. He controlled water — he could call rain from clear skies and summon floods from dry riverbeds. Where his brother destroyed, he healed. Together they were complete.

After proving their power by cutting a great tree in half with a thrown weapon — a feat that left the people speechless with awe — the twins assured the village that no more monsters would trouble them.

They established that a messenger would circle the earth in one day to keep them informed of any new threats. The messenger was the wind itself, carrying news from every corner of the world to the twins' ears.

The twins then resumed their roles as protectors, watching from the sun and the moon, ready to descend if the people ever needed them again. The story explains the origin of the Apache Girls' Puberty Ceremony and the sacred relationship between the people and the Sun.
